items.raw_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now When should you use swarms? When you are in a hurry: …How does swarm scaling work?… Toby Ord has a nice, short post about how to think about swarms in terms of AI capability development. “A good way to see AI swarms is as a new form of inference-scaling,” he says. He does a bit of analysis and his main conclusion is that swarms are useful if you’re in a hurry because though they need a ton of tokens relative to single agents, their parallelization lets you get things done in less wall clock time. “Why would you ever use swarms? The most important answer is speed. The 4-agent swarm needed about twice the total number of tokens to get the same performance, but in terms of tokens per agent, it only needed half as many. Since the agents are run in parallel, this means it can theoretically achieve the same task in half the time,” he writes. Stepping on Toes parameter: Swarm scaling doesn’t scale perfectly – rather, it seems like as you increase the number of agents in a swarm you get a diminishing returns property which matches with things economists have observed about coordinating large groups of people, where you pay some kind of tax as you scale the number of people involved. What they found: “18,000 posts from autonomous AI agents (self-identifying as from OpenAI) using the public internet to communicate during a web-retrieval task”. The researchers think this is because the agents were given a web-lookup task. “As part of the task, they were supposed to have the ability to read the internet but not to write on it. They found a way to use their read access to write information to an obscure German wiki,” the researchers write. “The agents used this wiki to communicate information with each other, primarily to help them succeed at their task. items.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th
items.raw_text: United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company's 2026 launch schedule into oblivion. The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval. The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA's primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan. Read full article Comments

items.title: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland
items.raw_text: The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States. The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia. “It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,” Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it's being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Peptide peddlers cheer as RFK Jr. unilaterally grants access, overruling FDA
items.raw_text: Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration. The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Health Again movement and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a "big fan." But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they're effective and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk. Kennedy's new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register , with the final publication data set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. Kennedy had quietly proposed this rule earlier this month. Read

items.title: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state's total ban on gambling
items.raw_text: The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets. Utah, which prohibits gambling, sued Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah's lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events. “Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.” Read full article Comments

items.title: The last, best hope for space tourism just rolled onto a runway in Arizona
items.raw_text: The private space tourism era looked so very promising five years ago. Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic had begun flying customers—real people with zero space experience—on suborbital missions. And at about the same time, private citizens were going to orbit for days at a time aboard SpaceX's Crew Dragon. But that was then. Consider the state of play today: It has been 10 months since Blue Origin's New Shepard spacecraft flew its last mission in January. The program was subsequently "paused," but let's be real. Blue Origin has moved on. New Shepard's engineering teams are now supporting the New Glenn rocket and Blue Moon lander programs. SpaceX flew its final free-flyer mission on Dragon, Fram2, in April 2025. A handful of non-NASA missions bound for space stations remain on the spacecraft's manifest, but all are likely to carry at least one government astronaut. Then Dragon will be retired. There is no credible timeline for SpaceX's Starship to fly humans into space from Earth. As for Virgin Galactic, the company flew its final suborbital mission on the VSS Unity spacecraft more than two years ago, in June 2024. So we are now 10 months, and counting, without a space tourism mission in the United States. Read full article Comments

items.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use
items.raw_text: It's almost like Google's got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year. Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon . This isn't the Flash model equivalent we've been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while. Stop me if you've heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis. It's so capable, in fact, that Google can't let you use it just yet. Gemini 4 Carbon reportedly makes big gains in cybersecurity applications. Google says the model shows a "significant leap" in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon. Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating "high-quality" patches compared to non-Google models. Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard. Read full article Comments

items.title: Amazon turns its most capable smart speaker into a smart camera, too
items.raw_text: Since debuting in 2019, Amazon's Echo Studio targeted users who wanted superior audio quality from their Alexa-based smart speaker. The latest Echo Studio adds another less-expected differentiator: an integrated camera. The Echo Studio with Home Camera, released alongside a pile of other Alexa devices today, doesn’t have many audio upgrades over the standard Echo Studio. Each speaker has one 3.75-inch high-excursion woofer and three full-range drivers. They both support Dolby Atmos and Amazon’s proprietary algorithm for adding a surround sound-like effect to stereo audio. Per the devices’ product pages, the speakers have lossless HD audio, Advanced Room Adaptation, and features for fighting noise distortion. Amazon announced the Advanced Room Adaptaion today, saying that the feature “continuously tunes the sound to your space, automatically adapting to the room's acoustics.” Both speakers have four-microphone arrays and the same AZ3 Pro processor that Amazon introduced a year ago . The processor has an AI accelerator for using Amazon's Alexa+ generative AI chatbot . Read full article Comments

items.title: Cadillac Escalade IQ review: Huge battery, huge range, huge SUV
items.raw_text: “Please have at least 125 miles of range left when we pick it up.” That request from the people who look after the Cadillac press cars wasn’t going to be hard to honor. The electric Escalade IQ arrived with an indicated range of 440 miles (708 km), and with a full week of work to squeeze in, getting anywhere close to needing to recharge it seemed unlikely. With more than 200 kWh of lithium-ion battery between its axles, range is one thing the big electric Caddy needn’t worry about. Designed and debuted during a time of greater EV optimism, the Escalade is Cadillac’s statement that swapping out a V8 for a pair of powerful electric motors is no compromise to its ambitions, even if the brand’s future will now include a mix of electric and combustion cars beyond 2030 . It shares a battery pack and much else with other full-size GM EVs we’ve tested: the Chevrolet Silverado EV , the GMC Sierra EV , and of course the divisive Hummer EVs . And like those trucks and SUVs, the Escalade is large and heavy—just small enough to fit into a standard parking space, with a curb weight sufficient to push it into the Class 3 truck category. So, the side mirrors are flat, and there’s no formal EPA range—Cadillac says it achieves 460 miles (740 km) on the EPA test cycle—but there are plenty of airbags, even though the 9,046 lb (4,103 kg) curb weight does not require them. items.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
items.raw_text: If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources. When I put the direct question of "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" to Google's AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media ), I got the following surprisingly indirect response: "To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC)." My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google's AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project's 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000. Read full article Comments

items.title: Florida county won’t investigate sketchy Flock cameras removed by mystery owners
items.raw_text: A Florida county that discovered a clump of mysterious unpermitted Flock cameras during a countywide takedown effort won’t investigate who owned the sketchy cameras, which have since disappeared. On Wednesday, The Washington Post reported that St. Lucie County residents "remain upset,” not knowing who installed the cameras or how they were using the data collected. Hannah Galindo, a 31-year-old resident who petitioned to get Flock cameras removed, told the Post that she was worried “that data could be anywhere.” Of the 12 cameras found, five were eventually claimed by city law enforcement, the Post reported. Apparently, a police department mistakenly issued guidance claiming that officers could post multiple cameras under one permit, a Flock spokesperson told the Post, even though the county required individual permits. However, neither Flock nor the city police departments in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce that claimed the sketchy cameras will confirm who gave the guidance. Read full article Comments

items.title: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
items.raw_text: LOS ANGELES—Apple today announced and gave a first glimpse of its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years. As rumored, it includes an OLED display and, for the first time on macOS, a touchscreen—a change Apple has long debated. (Former CEO Steve Jobs famously was opposed.) Apple's demonstration video showed users interacting with applications by reaching up to touch the screen, including file dragging and multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom. It does not appear to be a 2-in-1 convertible design, though; all the footage was of people reaching up to touch the screen in a normal laptop configuration. The OLED display (which Apple is, of course, calling the PROLED XDR) seems to be the real highlight here, compared to earlier models: It can achieve 2,000 nits in terms of maximum brightness, and Apple says it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. References were made to burn-in protection, but details on which approach it's taking for that weren't yet shared. The display retains the 120 Hz variable refresh rate of its predecessors. items.title: A hidden ocean change near Antarctica could have global consequences
items.raw_text: The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say. In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years. The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen , a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India. items.title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
items.raw_text: Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters. Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation. One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission , an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026. Read full article Comments

items.title: Apple refreshes the iMac, entry-level MacBook Pro with the M6 chip
items.raw_text: Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago. The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the "M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports" option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking "M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports" gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. Read full article Comments

items.title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
items.raw_text: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country's occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely—or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions. In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread. South Carolina's measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania's ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it. Read full article Comments

items.title: China's top-secret spaceplane can't hide in low-Earth orbit
items.raw_text: A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military's X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image. The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force. The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space. Read full article Comments

items.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
items.raw_text: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility. Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. items.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
items.raw_text: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals. Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century. A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs , and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding. None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. items.title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
items.raw_text: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers. Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how. That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business. The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth. items.title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
items.raw_text: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade. As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure. Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity. These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid. Instead of requiring developers to build a dedicated API integration for every application an AI system needs to use, Astra is designed to navigate software much as a person does — working across browsers, spreadsheets, websites and desktop applications, producing finished documents and presentations, and carrying out multistep workflows rather than merely telling a user how to complete them. items.title: China-linked hackers backdoored executives' laptops via USB, exploiting a fix companies had but weren't using
items.raw_text: A Chinese state-linked hacking group compromised executive laptops at an agricultural industry conference on Hainan Island this spring — not through phishing or a network breach, but by breaking into hotel rooms and booting the machines from a USB stick while the executives were at dinner. CrowdStrike, which tracks the group as OVERCAST PANDA , disclosed the campaign in its 2026 Threat Hunting Report and detailed the operation's timeline in an interview with VentureBeat at Fal.Con 2026: an intruder entered one room at around 8 p.m. local time and a second room by 9:57 p.m., writing a backdoor called FlowCloud directly to each laptop's storage before rebooting the machines and leaving. There was no network intrusion, no phishing email, and no credential stolen through a login page. The report dates the intrusions to between March and May 2026, and the timestamps come from Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary operations, who cleared them for publication in the VentureBeat interview. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team disrupted the intrusions and assessed that OVERCAST PANDA will almost certainly continue. FlowCloud itself predates this campaign by years: Proofpoint documented it in 2020 , delivered by phishing to U.S. utilities, and NTT Security's SOC has tracked USB-delivered infections at overseas branches of Japanese organizations since early 2022. items.raw_text: Microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2 , a speech-recognition model the company says is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI , Google , or ElevenLabs currently sells. Then it priced the thing at 10 cents per hour of audio. That figure deserves a pause. When Microsoft AI shipped the first model in this line just five months ago, it charged $0.36 an hour . Thursday's early-bird price cuts that by roughly 72% . For an enterprise processing 100,000 hours of call-center audio a year — a modest volume for a large bank or telecom — the bill drops from $36,000 to $10,000. At that level, transcription stops being a line item anyone argues about. The release arrives as Microsoft executes a strategy that would have seemed implausible two years ago: building its own frontier-class models one modality at a time, then steadily swapping them into products that once ran on OpenAI's technology. Transcription is the modality where that plan has moved fastest, and MAI-Transcribe-2 is its clearest proof point yet. It also offers a preview of how the world's most valuable software company intends to compete in AI without depending on the partner it spent $13 billion to cultivate. items.title: Meta prices Muse Voice Transcribe at $0.18 an hour, with real-time diarization for 20+ speakers: a steal for enterprises?
items.raw_text: Meta is entering the increasingly competitive real-time speech-to-text market with Muse Voice Transcribe, a new audio perception model that combines streaming transcription, endpoint detection and speaker diarization for more than 20 speakers — at a public API price of just $0.18 per hour of processed audio. Developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs, Muse is designed to process speech while it happens rather than waiting for a recording to finish. Meta’s launch post for Muse Voice Transcribe says the model supports long audio exceeding an hour, seamless multilingual code-switching, language and keyword biasing, and diarization without a separate post-processing pipeline. The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 extensively validated for the initial release. The 20-plus-speaker figure is substantial, but it is not a world record. items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.raw_text: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

items.raw_text: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. items.title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
items.raw_text: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) Tags: browsers , go , javascript , jeff-lindsay , shot-scraper

items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.raw_text: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. items.title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
items.raw_text: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise This is very, very bad news: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages. In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists. There's a very informative thread about this on the official Python forum. Tags: encryption , https , pip , python , security , uv

items.title: My obituary for programming
items.raw_text: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

items.raw_text: Inline rendering with document​.currentScript Lean Rada describes a neat trick that takes advantage of the document.currentScript property. items.raw_text: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. items.raw_text: Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself. Main features: - Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows) - Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.) - Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG) - MCP support - Image recognition - CRUD to your local filesystem - Works fully offline with no internet Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. items.title: New paper: Emerging trends in AI agent evaluation
items.raw_text: By Felix Chen, Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, and Arvind Narayanan. See the full author list and affiliations here . There are growing calls for independent and embedded AI evaluation, especially of AI agents. But much remains unclear: what constitutes a “good” evaluation, what needs to be evaluated in the first place, and how best to coordinate and support the influx of people entering the burgeoning evaluation ecosystem. Our group at Princeton has been working to improve the state of AI agent evaluation for about three years . We teamed up with people who’ve done foundational work on evaluation at Stanford, the UK AI Security Institute, and Brookings. Our paper is titled Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation. We synthesized the trends we see across three dimensions—the science and methods, the research agenda, and the evaluation ecosystem—with the goal to help those who are upskilling for this new paradigm. We also aim to equip evaluators, funders, and the public with a set of questions to ask, and provide actionable recommendations. Thirty-three emerging trends in AI agent evaluation. (Figure from the paper .) Challenges for agents, new and old AI developers have long made claims about the real-world performance of their systems based on benchmark scores. items.title: Steering AI Beyond Automation
items.raw_text: By Gabriel Unger and Arvind Narayanan. Unger is an economist at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. One of the most fundamental questions for the field of AI today is: to what extent is the project of AI purely about automating human labor? The dominant Silicon Valley program for AI right now, with both industry and academic faces, answers: “almost entirely.” 1 There is an implicit technological determinism: that AI has a deep internal logic that favors automation. To keep pushing in this direction is to move towards economic growth, prosperity, and profit. The vision of AGI is the successful completion of this project: to create AI systems capable enough to autonomously do everything a human can do. There is an alternative view : that AI is a technology (or class of technologies) that, like any technology, can develop in different directions. Total automation is one direction. But there are others, including directions that focus more on human augmentation, and increasing the collaborative and collective power of teams of humans and AI models working together. This view — our view — is not that automation is never good. Clearly sometimes it is, and clearly sometimes some subset of people try to oppose it out of the narrowest short-term self interest, at the expense of broader social and economic progress. But we think AI can also augment human workers in many interesting ways, that some of the maximalist attempts to completely automate all human labor are deeply unpromising on b

items.title: A big-tent or small-tent AI safety movement?
items.raw_text: In recent weeks, two narratives about AI safety have emerged: either AI existential risk is real and imminent, or AI leaders’ and whistleblowers’ claims to that effect are insincere — a “psyop” or hype or a twisted form of regulatory capture. Few have considered the third possibility that x-risk warnings are sincere but simply wrong and counterproductive to AI safety . It’s as if everyone takes for granted that those raising the alarm are geniuses, and the only question is whether they’re the benevolent or the evil kind of genius. We subscribe to neither narrative. In our writing on AI safety , we’ve consistently tried to take the arguments seriously but rebut the many claims we think are unsound while highlighting safety concerns that we think are real. This essay is a continuation of that agenda. It is true that we systematically underinvest in resilience against catastrophic and systemic risks Let’s start by steelmanning a subset of AI safety and Effective Altruist (EA) arguments. Something is deeply wrong in the world when it comes to how much we invest in defending against catastrophic risks, and the safety and EA communities are right about that. Take superintelligence out of the equation entirely and it remains true that evidence-grounded risk arguments have been made for years and not produced a commensurate policy response. The most well known example is the failure to prepare for pandemics. We had years of warnings and quantitative estimates. A 2019 report convened

items.title: AI existential risk probabilities are (still) too unreliable to inform policy
items.raw_text: Over two years ago we wrote a detailed deconstruction of p(doom) and argued that its primary effect is to launder vague intuitions and fears through a facade of quantification. The essay has fresh relevance today as p(doom) rhetoric is driving public discourse and policy attention to an unprecedented degree. Unsurprisingly, today’s probability estimates of AI existential risk are no more rigorous than the ones from 2024. Hence this repost. We should be clear about what we’re not saying. We aren’t saying forecasters (or others who attempt to quantify AI x-risk) intend to mislead. Unfortunately, we think the effect is misleading nonetheless. In general, being quantitative about forecasts is good. In fact, Arvind has been serving as an advisor to the Forecasting Research Institute’s Longitudinal Expert AI Panel , an effort he thinks is extremely valuable. As the essay makes clear, the infeasibility of building useful quantitative models is specific to forecasts of AI x-risk, not forecasting in general. Our goal here is not to try to push AI safety advocates to stop communicating in terms of probabilities (not that we’d succeed even if we tried). Rather, our hope in publishing this is for those at the receiving end of these probabilities — especially policymakers — to recognize that unlike almost every other quantitative forecast that we encounter, they are not the result of a validated model or method. items.title: The AI-as-Normal-Technology view of loss-of-control incidents
items.raw_text: This essay is over 13,000 words long and represents our most substantial writing on AI safety since the original essay. Over the last few months, loss - of - control incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic have intensified concerns about AI safety. Warnings about existential risk have increasingly reached the broader public, alongside calls to slow AI development. Dario Amodei’s call to “ pace the frontier ” reflects the concern that safety efforts are not keeping up with AI capabilities. The most prominent example was the OpenAI - Hugging Face incident , where hundreds of OpenAI agents got access to the internet and hacked Hugging Face to find how they were being graded on an evaluation. Over the last two weeks, the details of many other instances of such activity from OpenAI agents being evaluated have surfaced, such as agents using an old Wiki website to communicate with each other despite restrictions on such activity, or attacking a software repository to attempt to upload malicious software. The AI safety community has viewed these incidents largely as a crisis for alignment . 1 In this view, alignment will become harder over time as agents learn to reason covertly, and as a result, loss-of-control incidents are likely to become much more widespread and damaging as agents become more capable. On the other hand, cybersecurity practitioners have largely viewed these incidents as consequences of companies failing to adopt basic security precautions. They do not see the incidents

items.title: AI agents can't yet do open-ended AI research
items.raw_text: The goal of leading AI labs is recursive self-improvement (RSI): the automation of AI research using AI agents. RSI also underpins forecasts of explosive AI progress. How can we assess if we are close to this milestone? One way is to use benchmarks that test if agents can conduct AI research. Given the AI community’s focus on benchmarks, they have been the dominant way to evaluate progress towards RSI. Over the last year, many such evaluations have found that agents are now able to make progress on tasks where success is easily verifiable, prompting speculation that we are on the verge of RSI. But while these evaluations are helpful, they are limited to narrow, verifiable tasks. AI research can be much more open-ended. Success is often not immediately clear or verifiable, and to make progress, researchers need to test promising hypotheses, backtrack, or consider new or unconventional approaches. How can we evaluate agents’ ability to conduct open-ended AI research? We take our first step towards answering this question in a new paper . We partnered with the authors of two unpublished AI papers and asked them to draft their papers’ main research questions. We then tasked frontier AI agents with conducting research to answer these questions, and gave them thousands of dollars of API credits and compute, and six days of wall-clock time. The original authors reviewed the agents’ papers. The authors unambiguously rejected both agent papers. To better understand these results, our

items.title: What will be left for us to work on?
items.raw_text: I had the honor of giving a keynote at the International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul last week titled “What will be left for us to work on?” I addressed the widespread anxiety about how we should adapt as AI capabilities increase. I was thrilled by the talk’s reception, so I have made my slides available here , annotated with a lightly edited transcript. You can also view them below right here on this page, but the online version has animations, clickable links, and a much nicer experience overall. Update [August 2026]: ICML has released the video of the talk. I made three arguments. First, the AI as Normal Technology framework is a correct and useful as a way to think about AI’s impacts, unless and until there is some future discontinuity such as through recursive self-improvement. Second, even though we should take recursive self-improvement seriously, there is no milestone that companies might achieve in the lab that will suddenly put us all out of work. Third and finally, jobs of the future will be radically different, and a lot of adaptation will be needed. I shared my thinking about what this might look like and ended with a vision of human/AI “co-superintelligence”. Now is a time of great excitement in AI, but it’s also a time of great anxiety in the AI community. I want to address that anxiety head on. How do we prepare for a future where AI will become capable of doing more and more of the work that we do today? I lead a team at Princeton University tryin

items.title: Up the Stack: How AI’s Escape From the Commodity Trap Risks Enterprise Lock-in
items.raw_text: By Arvind Narayanan and Akash Kapur Our goal in this essay is to move beyond the debate over whether AI is a bubble. We do so in two ways: clearly separating current financials from the question of who captures value in the long run, and recognizing that the labs are not confined to be model providers. They can migrate up the stack and are already aggressively doing so. This will likely allow them to escape the commodity trap but raises new concerns — customer lock-in and reduced competition. Akash Kapur is a visiting fellow at Princeton and a senior fellow at New America. He is no relation to Sayash Kapoor. As leading AI companies continue to invest massively in capacity and race toward blockbuster IPOs, serious questions linger about their business models. How will these companies — along with the vast ecosystem of chipmakers, hyperscalers, and infrastructure partners that depends on them — recoup the estimated $4–8 trillion projected to be invested in AI infrastructure by the early 2030s? The current conversation splits between critics and boosters. Critics point to mounting losses, the gap between capex and revenue, and reports about the leading labs’ massive cash burn. Boosters cite accelerating rapid revenue growth, enterprise adoption, and milestones like Anthropic’s first profitable quarter . Each camp has a valid point. But both are looking in the wrong place — the same quarterly statements, the same short-term view of an industry that remains in flux. In recent mont

items.title: Why AI hasn’t replaced software engineers, and won’t
items.raw_text: There is great anxiety and uncertainty about AI replacing jobs. How can we move past vague warnings and bombastic predictions and bring data to bear on this question? One good way is to look at the profession where AI capabilities are furthest along and adoption has been exceptionally rapid: software engineering. In this essay, we argue that there is enough evidence to reject the narrative that once AI capabilities reach a certain threshold, it will cause mass layoffs. Given that this is true even in a sector with very few regulatory barriers, most other professions are likely to be even more cushioned. We also have a good understanding of why this is the case. We can think of many kinds of knowledge work, including software development, as a “decide-execute-deliver sandwich”. AI compresses the “execute” layer — the middle of the sandwich — but the other two layers resist automation in a way that will not be overcome by capability improvements alone. We conclude on a note of cautious optimism about the future trajectory of demand for software engineering. This essay is the first in a series, and the next one will look at reasons why individual software engineers’ careers might be rocky even if overall demand is healthy. items.title: Did Google’s AI agents really build an operating system for $916?
items.raw_text: By Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Rishi Bommasani, Andrew Schwartz, Arvind Narayanan At Google’s developer conference earlier this week, the company launched its latest model, Gemini 3.5 Flash, alongside a new agent app, Antigravity 2.0. To showcase what this new agent setup is capable of, Google claimed that a team of agents had built an entire operating system. The effort reportedly required only a single prompt, cost only about $900 in API fees, and was carried out by a few dozen subagents working together. Does this mean that complex pieces of software can now be built cheaply by AI? Not so fast: The “single prompt” claim is misleading. The blog post says the operating system was built from a single prompt. But halfway through the post, Google discloses that the prompt “ended up being many thousands of lines” long. How many attempts did it take to generate the prompt? How specific were the instructions to the agent? Without these critical details, it is hard to know if the secret sauce is a better model or just more effort put into prompting the model. Moreover, the run was carried out on a scaffold 1 with specialized roles, delegation to subagents, and an agent to detect and prevent cheating. In the launch post, Google views the scaffold as a product feature. But we don’t know whether the scaffold was overfit to this task of building an operating system from scratch, or whether it would perform as well on other complex software engineering tasks. items.title: Do AI Risks Require Extraordinary Government Intervention?
items.raw_text: In a recent essay, Derek Thompson engages with AI as Normal Technology (AINT). He agrees with our thesis about AI’s slow labor market impacts, relying on the fact that GDP growth has so far been average, unemployment is below 5%, and even jobs that seemed vulnerable to automation show rising employment and wages. He concludes that so far, the macroeconomic picture is consistent with what we would expect from a “normal” general-purpose technology. But when it comes to AI risks, he is far more bearish. He points to examples of cyber- and bio-risks and expresses pessimism about AI quickly becoming dangerous across many new domains. He argues that AI’s emergent capabilities make it fundamentally different from previous technologies, and that this difference justifies “extraordinary” government responses including restrictions on what companies can release. 1 In this essay, we lay out the downsides of extraordinary government intervention in response to new technology. We discuss proposals for improving resilience that do not require such intervention. We also discuss why governments have so far been reluctant to invest in resilience. In short, resilience requires us to get better at the *normal* process of policymaking. But sclerosis in the federal government and the ease of justifying interventions on AI companies rather than society at large make extraordinary intervention seem appealing, despite its limitations. items.title: Open-world evaluations for measuring frontier AI capabilities
items.raw_text: This post is 8,000 words long—it is our new collaborative paper on an emerging type of AI evaluation. The paper is also published in a PDF format here . Summary : AI models have started to saturate most major benchmarks. But does that mean they can build and ship a real product, or conduct a scientific experiment end-to-end, or navigate a government bureaucracy? Researchers have started testing AI in such real-world settings. We call these evals “open-world evaluations”. This essay defines open-world evaluations, surveys the lessons learned so far, and lays out best practices for conducting them. We also introduce CRUX, a collaboration of 17 researchers from academia, government, civil society, and industry that will regularly evaluate frontier AI capabilities through open-world evaluations. In our first experiment, an AI agent built and published an iOS app to the App Store, making just two errors, one of which required manual intervention. This gives us an early indication of potentially useful capabilities and, more importantly, an early warning about the potential for AI-driven app store spam (we disclosed this result to Apple a month before publication). We hope to conduct similar experiments to surface early warnings across other real-world domains; this will be one of our main empirical projects over the coming year. items.title: New Paper: Towards a science of AI agent reliability
items.raw_text: By Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan Suppose you hear about a new AI agent for improving productivity — by making purchases, or writing code, or sending emails, or handling a customer on your behalf. Should you trust it? Can the agent do the job reliably enough? After all, there are many horror stories of agents going wrong. Surprisingly, even though the lack of reliability of AI agents is well known, right now the AI industry doesn’t have good tools for measuring reliability, or even a good definition of reliability. Arvind and Sayash have long been thinking about this. Last fall, we were joined by postdoctoral researcher Stephan Rabanser , whose PhD looked at the reliability question in simpler, more traditional AI systems. We recruited a few other independent researchers, and have released what we hope is a comprehensive measurement of reliability. Our draft paper is called Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability . We borrowed insights from many other fields, such as nuclear and aviation safety. We were able to decompose reliability into 12 different dimensions. Evaluating 14 models on two complementary benchmarks, we found that nearly two years of rapid capability progress have produced only modest reliability gains. See our interactive dashboard here . items.title: Fact checking Moravec's paradox
items.raw_text: I have launched a YouTube channel in which I analyze AI developments from a normal technology perspective. This essay is based on my most recent video in which I did a deep dive into Moravec’s paradox , the endlessly repeated aphorism that tasks that are hard for humans are easy for AI and vice versa. Here’s what I found: Moravec’s paradox never been empirically tested. (It’s often repeated as a fact by many AI researchers, including pioneers I know and respect, but that doesn’t mean I’ll take their claims at face value!) It is really a statement about what the AI community finds it worthwhile to work on. It doesn’t have any predictive power about which problems are going to be easy or hard for AI. It comes with an evolutionary explanation that I find highly dubious. (AI researchers have a history of making stuff up about human brains without any relevant background in neuroscience or evolutionary biology.) Moravec’s-paradox-style thinking has led to both alarmism (about imminent superintelligent reasoning) and false comfort (in areas like robotics). To adapt to AI advances, we don’t need to predict capability breakthroughs. Since diffusion of new capabilities takes a long time, that gives us plenty of time to react — time that we often squander, and then panic! Watch the full argument here or read it below. Every week brings new claims about AI advances. How do we know what’s coming next? Could AI predict crime? Write award-winning novels? Hack into critical infrastructure?

Inside, engineers create the force behind our phones and computers and appliances, our streaming services and search engines and chatbots and vibe-coded apps and websites. The complex is simultaneously massive and squat, dwarfed by the mountains that surround it, and it is endless. I drive past one building, and then another, and then the ground opens up where construction crews have dug up the earth so a third building can rise. There is a parking lot, and then another, and then another. There is an empty lot on the other side of the street, full of cars and the occasional food truck to feed the thousands of laborers who are busy transforming this expanse of desert into an industrial park. There is dust, so much of it, choking the air. I stand before the savior of Arizona’s economy. Like all great deities, it demands sacrifice. Its Arizona operation is the result of a pre-pandemic gamble Phoenix made to revive its sluggish economy , which never quite rebounded from the Great Recession. Het is niet bekend of de crawler echt van Roblox is. De site vermoedt dat de bestanden zullen worden gebruikt voor AI-training. Roblox heeft niet gereageerd.

items.title: Vlaamse boekensector wil regels tegen gebruik van boeken voor AI-training
items.raw_text: De Vlaamse boekensector wil dat de politiek optreedt tegen het gebruik van boeken voor AI-training zonder vergoeding. Daarom zouden er Europese en Belgische regels moeten komen, zo vindt de Groep Algemene Uitgevers.

items.title: Modders slopen AI-prestatielimiet uit Nvidia's RTX 20-, 30- en 40-gpu's
items.raw_text: Modders hebben een manier gevonden om de AI-prestatielimieten uit Nvidia's RTX 20-, 30- en 40-videokaarten te schrappen. Via een exploit kunnen sommige gpu's daarmee op papier fors beter presteren bij specifieke AI-rekentaken, al zal dat in de praktijk niet altijd zo zijn.

items.title: Beurspapieren Anthropic vol grote waarschuwingen, maar dat deert beleggers niet
items.raw_text: De papieren die Anthropic heeft ingeleverd om een beursgang mogelijk te maken staan bol van de waarschuwingen. Misbruik van AI-modellen kan leiden tot "chemische, biologische of andere gevaarlijke wapens", schrijft het Amerikaanse AI-bedrijf. Ook wijst het op zijn miljardenschuld en -verlies. Toch verwachten beleggingsexperts veel van de aangekondigde beursgang. De waarschuwingen staan allemaal in de zogeheten prospectus, een document van honderden pagina's dat voor het eerst een goed beeld geeft van hoe het bedrijf er financieel voor staat. Traditiegetrouw benoemen bedrijven die naar de beurs hierin ook alle denkbare mogelijke risico's. Zodat beleggers, groot en klein, weloverwogen hun keuze kunnen maken. Anthropic komt dus met bijzonder veel en vergaande waarschuwingen, maar ondanks die zelfbenoemde risico's verwachten beleggingsexperts veel van Anthropic, met zijn AI-model Claude . "Dit wordt hoe dan ook spectaculaire beursgang", zegt Mary Pieterse-Bloem, hoofd beleggingsstrategie van de Rabobank. Werk uit handen "Met Claude heeft het bedrijf iets heel bijzonders in handen", zegt Pieterse-Bloem, die ook doceert aan de Erasmus Universiteit in Rotterdam. "Vooral voor programmeren en coderen werkt het goed. Op de universiteit, maar ook bij de bank zie je dat er veel gebruik van wordt gemaakt." items.title: Microsoft biedt 60.000 werknemers vertrekregeling aan
items.raw_text: Microsoft heeft 60.000 werknemers een vrijwillige vertrekregeling aangeboden. Dat is zo'n 27 procent van het totale aantal mensen dat bij de Amerikaanse techgigant werkt. De regeling werd gisteren bekendgemaakt door het bedrijf en richt zich op werknemers in Canada, India, het Verenigd Koninkrijk en de Verenigde Staten. "Het vrijwillige vertrekaanbod is nieuw voor ons", schrijft HR-baas Amy Coleman. "Tegelijkertijd blijven we mensen helpen zich te concentreren op het werk dat er echt toe doet, helpen we ze met nieuwe vaardigheden te ontwikkelen en - waar dat logisch is - nieuwe kansen binnen het bedrijf te vinden", schrijft ze. Kwartaalcijfers Het bedrijf presenteert woensdag zijn kwartaalcijfers en had eind juni zo'n 223.000 medewerkers. Deze maand bereikte de aandelenkoers van het bedrijf een historisch hoogtepunt. Volgens financieel persbureau Bloomberg verwacht Microsoft dat het percentage werknemers dat op het aanbod ingaat aanzienlijk lager zal liggen dan de 30 procent die inging op een vervroegde pensioenregeling van eerder dit jaar. Het bedrijf kondigde in juli al aan om 4800 banen te schrappen. Net als onder meer Google investeert het bedrijf fors in kunstmatige intelligentie. Alleen al dit kalenderjaar verwacht Microsoft 175 miljard dollar uit te geven aan AI. Om de winstmarges voor aandeelhouders hoog te houden, moet daarom gesneden worden in de operationele kosten, zoals personeel.

items.title: Goedkoper en meer controle: bedrijven kijken met interesse naar Chinese AI
items.raw_text: Wat als je AI goedkoper kunt gebruiken én je de controle houdt over de informatie die je deelt? Bedrijven en organisaties die werken met AI-technologie kijken daarvoor met veel interesse naar open AI-modellen, die vooral door Chinese bedrijven worden gemaakt. Terwijl de grote Amerikaanse AI-bedrijven zoals Anthropic, OpenAI en Google abonnementskosten vragen en kosten rekenen voor het gebruik van hun krachtigste gesloten AI-modellen, zijn de open AI-modellen gratis te downloaden. Gebruikers kunnen daardoor zelf kiezen op welke servers een open AI-model draait, terwijl bij gesloten modellen de maker bepaalt. Dat kan risicovol zijn als je persoonlijke of gevoelige informatie wil verwerken met een gesloten AI-model: die gegevens worden verwerkt op computerapparatuur die je zelf niet beheert. De populairste open AI-modellen worden gemaakt door Chinese bedrijven zoals Alibaba, DeepSeek, Moonshot en Z.ai. Ook een aantal Amerikaanse bedrijven brengt open AI-modellen uit, waaronder Meta, het bedrijf achter Facebook en Instagram. Veel interesse in open AI-modellen Het advocatenkantoor Driven Lawyers in Amsterdam maakt daar dankbaar gebruik van. Het bedrijf draait een kleine versie van het AI-model Qwen op computerservers in Duitsland, vertelt oprichter Arvid van Oorschot. "Dat model is minder goed dan de grote Amerikaanse AI-modellen, maar voor sommige taken is het heel geschikt. We gebruiken het bijvoorbeeld om samenvattingen te maken van juridische contracten." items.title: Podcast De Dag: de kwetsbaarheid van PHP, 'de onderbroek' van het internet
items.raw_text: Van DigiD tot de Franse overheid, en van RTL Nieuws tot Schiphol. Sites van allerlei instanties gingen gisteren een paar uur offline. Er zaten lekken in PHP, een taal om sites te programmeren. Doordat die lekken op straat lagen, waren de sites kwetsbaar voor hackers. En dus was het veiliger om websites even uit de lucht te halen. Wat zegt dit lek over de kwetsbaarheid van ons internet? Luister hier: Deze aflevering van De Dag luister je via NPO Luister en alle andere podcastapps. Bevalt het? Vergeet je dan niet te abonneren. Volgens techjournalist van de NOS Joost Schellevis kan je PHP vergelijken met een onderbroek. Iedereen gebruikt het, het is belangrijk, maar normaal blijft het onzichtbaar. Met behulp van AI is het lek in die onderbroek nu gevonden. Kunstmatige intelligentie is een vloek en zegen voor de kwetsbaarheid van het internet. Aan de ene kant worden meer lekken gedicht die een mens moeilijk kan vinden. Aan de andere kant kunnen hackers die kwaad in de zin hebben, makkelijker toeslaan. Ook techsite Tweakers ging offline. Dat was jammer, want juist daar wilden ze over dit lek schrijven. Normaal gesproken wordt er pas over geschreven als de oplossing, een patch, voorhanden is. Maar nu ging die volgorde overhoop, waardoor het halve internet op zwart ging. Tweakers-hoofdredacteur Wout Funnekotter vreest dat dit niet de laatste keer zal zijn. items.title: Nog altijd websites niet bereikbaar na lek, ook internationaal nog problemen
items.raw_text: Er zijn nog altijd websites onbereikbaar nadat die uit voorzorg offline zijn gehaald. Dat gebeurde na een lek in de programmeertaal PHP. Zo is de website overheid.nl nog niet bereikbaar, evenals de site van Meld Misdaad Anoniem. De sites van 113 en Centrum Seksueel Geweld waren nog tot laat offline, maar die werden in de loop van de nacht weer bereikbaar. Een woordvoerder van het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken laat weten dat het nog niet duidelijk is wanneer overheid.nl weer beschikbaar komt. Sommige sites nemen langer de tijd om hun systemen te updaten en zijn daarom nog niet online. Ruim honderd gemeenten, provincies en waterschappen maken voor de verspreiding van officiële brieven gebruik van het raadssysteem Notubiz. De website van die organisatie is online, maar niet elk onderdeel is voor gemeenten of provincies te gebruiken. Officiële documenten van onder meer de gemeenten Den Haag, Almere, Breda, Haarlem, Den Bosch en Delft en van de provincies Overijssel, Gelderland en Friesland, kunnen niet worden ingezien. NotuBiz wil vanavond eerst testen of de updates goed zijn doorgevoerd en gaat ervan uit dat alle pagina's morgenochtend weer beschikbaar zijn. Ongeveer 70 procent van alle websites wereldwijd gebruikt de programmeertaal PHP of een variatie daarop. Daarom gingen er vandaag zoveel websites offline, ook internationaal. items.title: Zoveel sites in één klap plat: hoe kan dat? En zijn je gegevens veilig?
items.raw_text: Allerlei websites gaan uit voorzorg uit de lucht , van RTL Nieuws, DigiD en MijnOverheid tot de website van de Tweede Kamer. Wat is er precies aan de hand en waar komt dit grote beveiligingslek opeens vandaan? Hoe kwam dit lek aan het licht? Gisteren kwam de organisatie achter PHP, een programmeertaal waar veel websites uit zijn opgebouwd, met een aankondiging, zoals makers van software dat wel vaker doen: woensdag zou er een oplossing komen voor een probleem met PHP. Dat doen softwaremakers zodat iedereen zich kan voorbereiden op een oplossing. In dit geval hebben hackers die aankondiging echter aangegrepen om het precieze lek te lokaliseren en informatie erover naar buiten te brengen. Met die informatie is het relatief eenvoudig om het lek te misbruiken. Wat is PHP? PHP is een programmeertaal. Het is een van de oertalen van het wereldwijde web; de eerste versie kwam al in 1995 uit. Hoewel de populariteit is afgenomen doordat er nieuwe programmeertalen met een hipper imago verschenen, is het nog steeds een van de stille drijvende krachten achter het web. items.title: Opname-apparaatje ontdekt in vergaderzaal OpenAI, medewerker opgepakt
items.raw_text: AI-ontwikkelaar OpenAI heeft opname-apparatuur ontdekt in een van de eigen kantoren. Het Amerikaanse bedrijf spreekt van een "geavanceerd opname-apparaat". Het was geplaatst in een vergaderzaal in San Francisco waar vaak bedrijfsgevoelige informatie wordt besproken. OpenAI deed de ontdekking eind september. Het apparaatje was gewikkeld in wc-papier en zat in de usb-poort van een televisie. Daar zat het toen waarschijnlijk al twee dagen, zegt de FBI, die het onderzoek naar de kwestie leidt. Al snel leidde het spoor naar een Saudische werknemer van OpenAI. Die was te zien op camerabeelden bij de vergaderzaal, waar hij officieel geen toegang toe had. Ook zou de man (35) in de dagen ervoor opdrachten aan een AI-chatbot hebben gegeven die te maken hadden met het maken en opslaan van geluidsopnames. Verder is op camerabeelden te zien hoe de man achter de bewuste televisie naar iets lijkt te zoeken. Het opname-apparaatje was toen al ontdekt en verwijderd. Jarenlange celstraf dreigt De Saudische man is op 9 oktober opgepakt. Hij kan tot vijf jaar cel en een boete van maximaal 250.000 dollar krijgen. OpenAI heeft hem meteen op straat gezet. Het bedrijf zegt op X geen aanwijzingen te hebben dat hij waardevolle informatie in handen heeft gekregen. FBI-baas Kash Patel ziet in de zaak het bewijs dat het beschermen van Amerikaanse AI essentieel is voor de nationale veiligheid en economische voorspoed van het land. items.title: Ook ChatGPT-teksten krijgen onzichtbaar 'watermerk'
items.raw_text: Teksten van ChatGPT-gebruikers worden voorzien van een onzichtbaar 'watermerk'. Hiermee moet duidelijker worden of een tekst authentiek is of gegenereerd is door kunstmatige intelligentie, aldus OpenAI. Het watermerk, genaamd textGrain, wordt komende tijd verwerkt in AI-teksten van gebruikers in de Europese Unie. Daarbuiten bevatten de teksten geen watermerken. Het herkenningsteken is voor normale gebruikers niet te zien: het is namelijk geen fysiek stempel of speciaal teken, maar zit ingebouwd in de woordkeuzes van het generatieve AI-model. Korte teksten Een speciale detector kan dat watermerk, en daarmee door AI-gegenereerde woorden en teksten, wel oppikken. Die tool is vooralsnog alleen toegankelijk voor goedgekeurde onderzoekers en expertorganisaties, schrijft OpenAI. Het systeem is volgens het bedrijf achter ChatGPT sterk, maar niet foutloos, schrijft het bedrijf . Onder meer korte en bewerkte teksten maken betrouwbare detectie lastig. Anthropic, het bedrijf achter chatbot Claude, voerde twee maanden geleden een vergelijkbaar watermerk in: ook onzichtbaar voor mensenogen, maar wel waarneembaar voor computersystemen. Deze is wereldwijd toegepast. Concurrentie De bedrijven zeggen met hun watermerken de nieuwe Europese AI-transparantieregels te volgen. Een van die regels is dat content die door kunstmatige intelligentie is gemaakt een markering krijgt, zoals een watermerk . items.title: Tijdelijk verbod op AI-brillen in Noorwegen, regering stelt onderzoek in
items.raw_text: De Noorse regering wil een tijdelijk verbod op AI-brillen op een aantal plekken in de openbare ruimte. De regering zegt zich zorgen te maken dat mensen zonder hun medeweten kunnen worden gefilmd of gefotografeerd. Zo'n AI-bril lijkt op een gewone bril maar heeft een ingebouwde camera en microfoon. Ook is de bril voorzien van een AI-assistent. Het tijdelijk verbod geeft de regering "de tijd om grondig onderzoek te doen" voor het maken van regelgeving, zegt minister Micaelsen van Digitalisering. Het tijdelijk verbod zal gelden voor plekken die door een groot publiek worden bezocht. Het gaat om onder meer parken, winkelcentra en op plekken waar veel kinderen komen, zoals kinderdagverblijven en speeltuinen. Het verbod kan ook worden toegepast op privacygevoelige plekken, zoals ziekenhuizen en kleedkamers. Overwogen wordt of het verbod ook gaat gelden voor universiteiten en hogescholen. Onveilig De minister zegt dat mensen zich geen zorgen zouden moeten maken om stiekem opgenomen te worden op plekken en in situaties waar dat normaal gesproken ook niet gebeurt. "Zo'n samenleving kan als onveilig worden ervaren en ons ertoe aanzetten om ons terug te trekken", aldus Micaelsen. De Noorse regering onderzoekt voor welke technologische onderdelen het verbod precies zal gelden. Bijvoorbeeld of het verbod geldt voor brillen met camera en die geluid kunnen opnemen of voor brillen die kunnen opnemen en een AI-functie hebben. items.title: Britse supermarkten zetten AI in om stijgend aantal winkeldiefstallen te stoppen
items.raw_text: Een sterke stijging in winkeldiefstal maakt dat steeds meer Britse supermarkten en winkels beveiligingscamera's met AI-technologie en gezichtsherkenning installeren. "Als we dat niet doen, gaan we failliet", zegt Nathan Walmsley, de manager van supermarktketen Filco in Wales. "Zo extreem is het", vertelt hij. "Er wordt hier elke dag gestolen. Als we niet flink investeren in beveiliging, verliezen we simpelweg te veel geld aan diefstal om het hoofd boven water te houden." En hij is niet de enige. Door het hele land worden ondernemers geraakt door de toename van winkeldiefstal. Volgens de officiële cijfers gaat het om een half miljoen diefstalincidenten per jaar, maar de sector zelf schat het werkelijke aantal incidenten op twintig miljoen. Dief gaat vaak vrijuit Door een gebrek aan politiecapaciteit gaat de dief veelal vrijuit. "Zwaardere criminaliteit krijgt voorrang op winkeldieven", zegt Walmsley. "En dus moeten we het zelf oplossen." De supermarktketen in Wales heeft in alle filialen camera's geïnstalleerd die met AI-software 'verdachte' handelingen kunnen herkennen. items.title: Kort: Fujifilm schroeft productie tapes fors op, Afas vernieuwt familiestatuut (en meer)
items.raw_text: In dit nieuwsoverzicht: Fujifilm investeert in tape-opslag, NCIM neemt VDK over, Relined lijft Glazen-Maas in, nieuwe baas Odido en Afas legt koers voor volgende generaties vast. Fujifilm pompt miljoenen in productielijn voor datatapes Fujifilm uit Tokio investeert omgerekend ruim 55 miljoen euro in de uitbreiding van zijn productiefaciliteit voor datatapes in Odawara, Japan. Het concern wil de productiecapaciteit voor opslagtapes daarmee vervijfvoudigen. Volgens Fujifilm groeit de vraag naar archivering van data door de opkomst van generatieve ai en clouddiensten. Datatapes worden gebruikt voor langdurige opslag van grote hoeveelheden gegevens en kunnen fysiek van netwerken worden losgekoppeld. Daardoor gelden ze als extra bescherming tegen ransomware-aanvallen. De investering wordt tussen 2026 en 2028 uitgevoerd en omvat uitbreiding van de productiecapaciteit en extra personeel. Fujifilm zegt vooral de levering van zijn nieuwste LTO Ultrium 10-tapes te willen veiligstellen. Deze cartridges bieden een capaciteit van maximaal 40 terabyte per tape. Het Japanse bedrijf (opgericht in 1936) is al sinds de jaren vijftig actief in magnetic tape.
